title: The Long Queue
subtitle: Voting machines stall at three booths; a four-hour queue is being called sabotage
coldOpen: 09:00. Three polling booths report stalled machines.
11:30. Queues reach four hours in the sun.
A post says the stalls are “only in opposition wards”.

briefing.grievance: Voters have waited four hours and some are leaving. They want working machines, water, and an answer to the claim that their ward was targeted.
knownFacts: Three of 42 booths reported machine faults; replacement units are at the records office.
The three booths are in two different wards with different leading parties.
Polling closes at 18:00; everyone in the queue at close is entitled to vote.
unverifiedClaims: A post says the faults are only in wards that vote against the government.
A message says the replacement machines are pre-loaded.
briefing.responsibility: You are the district election officer. Every voter in the queue has a right to vote, and every claim about the machines needs an answer.
briefing.objective: Replace the machines, keep every queued voter voting, and answer the targeting claim with facts.

rightsMoments.question: Polling closes at six, and six hundred voters are still queued after a machine fault. What does the law require?

options.text: Everyone already in the queue at closing time must be allowed to vote; the remedy fixes the fault, not the voters.
options.feedback: Correct. The right to vote is protected for those who turned up in time; delays caused by the system cannot be charged to them.

options.text: Close the doors at six; those outside can vote at a repoll.
options.feedback: Turning away queued voters disenfranchises people who did everything right.

options.text: Cancel the district’s poll so everyone is equal.
options.feedback: Cancelling valid votes to cure three booths is disproportionate.

rightsMoments.principle: Election rules protect every voter in the queue at closing time; remedies for faults must be proportionate and must not disenfranchise voters who turned up lawfully.
rightsMoments.why: Tokens at six let six hundred people vote; cutting the line would have turned a fault into a grievance.

simple.question: Voting closes at six. Six hundred people are still in line because of a fault. What must happen?

options.a: Everyone in the line at six gets to vote. Fix the fault, not the voters.
options.b: Close the doors at six. They can vote at a repoll.
options.c: Cancel the whole district’s vote so all are equal.

feedback.a: Yes! People who came on time keep their vote.
feedback.b: No. Sending them home takes away a vote they earned.
feedback.c: Cancelling good votes to fix three booths is unfair.

simple.principle: Everyone in the queue at closing time may vote. Fix the fault without punishing voters.
simple.why: Tokens at six let six hundred people vote. Cutting the line would have turned a fault into a grievance.
